channel.title: Sifon Imahjnr
channel.description: Essays, poems, and ideas from a software engineering and cybersecurity student.

item.title: Your Phone Knows You're Lonely Before You Do
item.description: Your phone doesn't need to read your messages to know how you're doing. It only needs to watch how you move, when you scroll, and how long you stay home.

item.title: YOU WOULD HAVE BEEN THERE TOO
item.description: Don’t act innocent. If you were there that day, you wouldn’t be the one crying at the cross. You’d be in the crowd. Yeah… you. The same mouth you use to pray? You would’ve used it to shout, “Crucify Him.”

item.title: The Art of Being Unseen
item.description: Not everything valuable is noticed, and not everything unnoticed is without worth. This is about learning to exist fully, even when no one is watching.

item.title: Why We Hold On to What Never Chose Us
item.description: We don’t always hold on because something was real, we hold on because it felt real to us. This is a quiet look at why letting go is less about them, and more about how we understand ourselves.

item.title: Your Password Is Already Out There. Here's How They Got It.
item.description: Hackers don't break into systems the way movies show you. They walk through doors you left open. Here's exactly how it happens, and what it means for you.

item.title: What AI Actually Means for People Like Us
item.description: Everyone is talking about AI like it's happening somewhere else, to someone else. It isn't. Here's what it actually means if you're young, from Africa, and building something in the middle of all this noise.

item.title: The Church Ain't Ready
item.description: I stepped into churches and choked on the silence. This is not a rejection of God

item.title: Security Is a Philosophy, Not a Feature
item.description: Most companies treat security like a checkbox. That's exactly why they keep getting breached. Security isn't something you install — it's something you think.

item.title: On Finishing Things
item.description: Starting is an act of optimism. Finishing is an act of discipline. Most people are better at one than the other, and the gap between them is where most good work goes to die.

item.title: The Gap Between Knowing and Doing
item.description: Understanding something completely and being able to do it are two different cognitive events. Most people collapse the distance between them and wonder why they're still stuck.

item.title: Notes on Learning Rust as Someone Who Thinks in Python
item.description: Switching languages is switching thought. Rust didn't just teach me a new syntax; it showed me everything Python had been quietly doing for me, and everything I had stopped thinking about because of it.

item.title: The Pages We Don’t Outgrow
item.description: Some people don’t leave with endings—they leave with absence. And somehow, that absence keeps echoing through every chapter that follows.

item.title: On Building in the Age of Noise
item.description: The internet doesn't just accelerate information — it accelerates forgetting. Building something that lasts requires understanding what you're actually building against.

item.title: Why Silence Is a Form of Thinking
item.description: We have made noise the default state of the mind, and called it productivity. But some of the most precise thinking happens in the absence of words.

item.title: The World Is Loud With Bad Advice
item.description: The world is loud with bad advice. Everyone wants to be a prophet with nothing holy in their mouths.

item.title: The Weight Beneath My Silence
item.description: I walk in daylight like the rest. But underneath the skin, there is a war the world was never meant to see.

item.title: Signal and Noise in an Age of Infinite Content
item.description: We have solved the problem of access. We have created the problem of discernment. On how to read, think, and choose in an era that does not reward slowness.

item.title: “Heaven Knows Why”
item.description: They said, “Heaven knows why.” And I almost laughed not because it was funny, but because it sounded like the kind of lie people tell when the truth is too ugly to say out loud.
